newsitem.title: GERMANY: German Henkel steps up pressure on Loctite.
newsitem.headline: German Henkel steps up pressure on Loctite.

text.p: German consumer products group Henkel KGaA said on Wednesday it was launching an offer for the 65 percent stake it does not already own in United States adhesives-maker Loctite Corp at $57.75 per share.
The bid, worth some $1.2 billion, was widely expected after Henkel's announcement last week that it had approached Loctite's board with an offer "at a price in the area of $56" (per share).
Loctite shares closed on Wall Street at $57-7/8 on Tuesday, marginally above the offer price and a level suggesting some market players were still hopeful of a higher bid.
But Henkel's board said in a statement on Wednesday it was still seeking to hold discussions with Loctite aimed at securing a friendly takeover of the company.

"It remains our preference to enter into a friendly, negotiated transaction with the management and board of Loctite, and it remains our fervent hope that we will be given the opportunity to so," Henkel chief executive Hans-Dietrich Winkhaus said in a statement, adding however that Loctite had so far not agreed to talks.
Henkel's bid is only valid if acceptances allow Henkel to increase its existing 35 percent stake past the 50 percent threshold that would give it control in Loctite.
In accordance with an agreement entered into between Henkel and Loctite two years ago, the offer will remain open until January 6 next year, twice the normal duration for such an offer.
Shares in Henkel closed 65 pfennigs higher at 69.95 in an overall stronger Frankfurt bourse after the announcement.
German share analysts said the ball was now in Loctite's court but said there was still room for Henkel to make a higher bid if need be.
"Henkel could, depending on the level of financing it gets, stretch to $59 or $60 a share," Brian Wilkinson, German equity analyst for HBSC James Capel in London said.

He added that German accounting rules relating to the booking of goodwill depreciation could allow it to bid higher without the deal diluting earnings according to the standard DVFA German accounting model.
"But in terms of commercial reality, $60 is about the maximum," he added.

The proposed deal has been widely applauded as reinforcing Henkel's leadership in the world market for industrial and commercial adhesives, but there was some concern about the impact it would have on Henkel's debt.
Such a deal would double Henkel's current debt levels, a fact which contributed to credit rating agency S&P's move to put the company on "CreditWatch" with negative implications last week.
Henkel has nonetheless said it plans to use debt to finance the planned acquisition to avoid having to make a rights issue.

Chemical sector analysts have also noted that Loctite earnings growth in the last four years has not been strong and that Loctite has not appeared to benefit greatly from the growth in demand for adhesives seen this year.
